title: THE GOD WHO BLED: THE TRUTH ABOUT JESUS THAT SHATTERS HUMAN LOGIC BUT HOLDS YOUR SALVATION TOGETHER
paragraphs: THE GOD WHO BLED: THE TRUTH ABOUT JESUS THAT SHATTERS HUMAN LOGIC BUT HOLDS YOUR SALVATION TOGETHER

How Could the Eternal God Become a Helpless Baby, Experience Hunger, Suffer on a Cross, and Die—Yet Never Stop Being God? The Answer Is Not a Contradiction. It Is the Miracle at the Heart of Your Redemption.
There is something deeply unsettling about the Christian faith that many people have heard their entire lives but have never truly stopped to consider.
The hands that formed the universe were once small enough to fit inside His mother's hands.
The One who gives breath to every living creature once took His first human breath.
The One who sustains all things experienced hunger.
The One who created the oceans became thirsty.
And the One through whom all things were made allowed Himself to be nailed to a wooden cross.
Think about that.
Not a prophet pretending to be God.
Not an angel wearing a human disguise.
Not a good man who eventually became divine.
God the Son Himself entered the human condition without surrendering His deity.
And that raises a question so profound that it has challenged theologians, troubled skeptics, confused sincere believers, and divided religious communities for centuries.
How can Jesus Christ be fully God and fully human at the same time?
Wouldn't that be a contradiction?
If God is eternal, how could Jesus be born?
If God is all-powerful, how could Jesus become exhausted?
If God cannot die, how could Jesus die on the cross?
And if Jesus was truly human, how could He possibly be God?
These are not foolish questions.
They are questions worth asking because Christianity does not merely claim that Jesus taught us how to live.
Christianity claims something infinitely greater.
The eternal Son of God became one of us so that sinners like us could be reconciled to God.
And if that claim is false, the entire Christian understanding of salvation collapses.
But if it is true?
Then Bethlehem was more than the birth of a remarkable child.
Calvary was more than the execution of an innocent man.
And the empty tomb was more than the ending of a tragic story.
It means the God against whom humanity sinned personally entered our broken world to accomplish the redemption we could never accomplish for ourselves.
Before we go any further, consider this question.
What if the very truth that seems hardest to understand about Jesus is the truth that makes your salvation possible?
Because the deeper we go into Scripture, the more astonishing the answer becomes.
The Gospel of John begins not with a manger, but with eternity.
John 1:1 declares:
"In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." (KJV)
The original Greek is breathtaking:
Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος.
En archē ēn ho logos, kai ho logos ēn pros ton theon, kai theos ēn ho logos.
Notice the extraordinary precision.
John does not say the Word began to exist in the beginning.
He says the Word was.
The Greek verb ἦν (ēn) describes the Word's existence at the beginning.
Before creation began, the Word already existed.
And John makes two truths clear.
The Word was with God, indicating personal distinction.
And the Word was God, affirming His divine identity.

The Greek construction does not mean that the Word was merely godlike or one lesser deity among many. Within John's monotheistic context, it identifies the Word as truly divine while distinguishing Him personally from the Father.
This matters because Christianity does not teach that Jesus is the Father.
The historic Christian confession is that the one God eternally exists as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
The Son is not the Father, yet the Son shares the one divine nature.
Then John delivers a statement that should stop every reader in their tracks.
John 1:14:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο.
Kai ho logos sarx egeneto.
"And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." (KJV)
Read that again.
The Word became flesh.
The Greek word σάρξ (sarx) means flesh. Here it emphasizes the reality of human existence, not merely a physical appearance.
And the verb ἐγένετο (egeneto) means "became."
The eternal Word, who already existed before creation, entered a new condition of existence as a genuine human being.
John does not say that the Word stopped being God.
He does not say that the Word merely appeared human.
He does not say that a human person was transformed into God.
He says that the Word became flesh.
This is the incarnation.
Not the subtraction of deity.
The assumption of humanity.
The Son did not cease to possess the divine nature when He took a human nature.
He remained what He eternally was while becoming what He had not previously been: truly human.
And that distinction changes everything.
Imagine someone asking you, "Can a person be both a father and a son?"
Of course.
There is no contradiction because the descriptions concern different relationships.
Now, that analogy cannot fully explain the incarnation. Human relationships are not the same as divine and human natures.
But it helps expose the central logical issue.
A contradiction would arise if Christians claimed that Jesus was both finite and infinite in exactly the same respect, or both created and uncreated according to the same nature.
That is not what historic Christianity teaches.
The Christian confession is that Jesus Christ is one divine Person, the eternal Son, who possesses two distinct natures: divine and human.
He is uncreated according to His divine nature.
He is born in time according to His human nature.
He is unlimited in divine power according to His deity.
He genuinely experiences human weakness according to His humanity.
These truths are extraordinary, but they are not formal contradictions.
A mystery is not automatically a contradiction simply because the human mind cannot exhaustively comprehend it.
The incarnation is not the claim that God became less than God.
It is the claim that the eternal Son truly became man without ceasing to be God.
And Scripture refuses to let us diminish either truth.
Colossians 2:9 declares:
"For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily." (KJV)
The Greek reads:
ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ κατοικεῖ πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος σωματικῶς.
Hoti en autō katoikei pan to plērōma tēs theotētos sōmatikōs.
There is a word here that deserves your attention.
θεότητος (theotētos).
It refers to deity or divine nature.
Paul is not saying that Jesus possesses a small portion of divinity.
He is not saying that Jesus merely reflects God's goodness.
He is saying that all the fullness of deity dwells in Christ bodily.
Not partially.
Not temporarily.
Not symbolically.
The fullness of deity.
And the word σωματικῶς (sōmatikōs) emphasizes bodily reality.
The same Christ who is truly divine is genuinely embodied.
This is why the Christian faith cannot reduce Jesus to a wise moral teacher.
A teacher can explain the way.
A prophet can announce the way.
But Jesus declares in John 14:6:
"I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me." (KJV)
He does not merely point toward reconciliation with God.
He is the mediator through whom reconciliation comes.
But here is where the doctrine becomes painfully personal.
Because understanding that Jesus is fully God and fully human is not merely about winning a theological debate.
It is about understanding why your suffering matters to Him.
Why your sin required His cross.
And why your worst failure does not have to be the final chapter of your life.
Consider what Hebrews says.
Hebrews 2:14 begins:
"Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same..." (KJV)
The original Greek contains the phrase:
καὶ αὐτὸς παραπλησίως μετέσχεν τῶν αὐτῶν.
Kai autos paraplēsiōs meteschen tōn autōn.
The point is profound.
Because the children share flesh and blood, Christ Himself truly participated in that human condition.
He did not save humanity by remaining distant from human experience.
He entered it.
Hebrews continues by explaining that through death He would defeat the devil's power associated with death and deliver those held in lifelong slavery through the fear of death.
Notice the logic.
He took flesh and blood because He came to die.
The incarnation was not an accidental detour on the road to redemption.
It was essential to the mission of the Redeemer.
God the Son did not become human because heaven had failed.
He became human because the saving purpose of God would be accomplished through His obedient life, sacrificial death, and victorious resurrection.
And suddenly, the manger and the cross belong to the same story.
The baby wrapped in swaddling clothes was born to live the human life we failed to live in perfect obedience.
The man who walked the dusty roads of Galilee would bear the sins of His people.
The One who slept in a boat would rise to command the storm.
The One who wept at Lazarus's tomb would call the dead man out.
And the One who cried out in suffering at Calvary would rise victorious from the grave.
Do you see the beauty?
His humanity was never an illusion.
His deity was never suspended.
Both are essential to the identity of the one Lord Jesus Christ.
And perhaps this is where someone reading needs to stop pretending.
Because you have been carrying something.
Something you have not told your family.
Something you hide behind your church attendance, your smile, your ministry involvement, or your social media posts.
Maybe you believe in Jesus intellectually.
But deep inside, you wonder whether He truly understands the pain of being human.
You wonder whether the Lord of glory understands what it means to be rejected.
To be misunderstood.
To be abandoned by friends.
To grieve.
To suffer.
To feel the crushing weight of human vulnerability.
Listen carefully.
The humanity of Jesus means that the Savior who reigns in heaven is no stranger to genuine human suffering.
Hebrews 2:17 says:

"Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people." (KJV)
The Greek uses the expression:
κατὰ πάντα τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς ὁμοιωθῆναι.
Kata panta tois adelphois homoiōthēnai.
To be made like His brothers and sisters in every respect relevant to His genuine humanity.
This does not mean Jesus shared our sinfulness.
Scripture explicitly teaches that He was without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
It means He truly entered human life, including its limitations, temptations, sorrows, and suffering, without committing sin.
And Hebrews 2:18 delivers an extraordinary promise:
"For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted." (KJV)
The Greek verb βοηθῆσαι (boēthēsai) means to help or come to someone's aid.
Jesus does not merely observe His struggling people from a distance.
He is able to help them.
Not because He has personally committed every sin they have committed.
He never sinned.
But because He has genuinely endured testing and suffering while remaining perfectly faithful.
His compassion is not theoretical.
His priesthood is not indifferent.
His humanity is real.
And His divine power is sufficient.
The One who understands your weakness is also the One powerful enough to save you.
But we must go deeper.
Because there is a question that cannot be ignored.
If Jesus is God, and God is immortal, how could Jesus die?
The answer is not that His divine nature ceased to exist.
God cannot cease to be God.
The answer is that the eternal Son truly experienced human death according to the human nature He had assumed.
Death, in ordinary human experience, is the separation of the soul from the body.
At the cross, Jesus truly died as a man.
His human body was laid in a tomb.
Yet His divine nature did not perish, and His divine Person did not cease to exist.
We must be careful here.
We are not saying that only a separate human person died while the Son of God remained uninvolved.
There are not two persons named Jesus.
There is one Lord Jesus Christ.
The Person who died is the eternal Son of God, and He died according to His human nature.
This is why Acts 20:28 can speak of God's church being purchased with His own blood, in a passage whose wording and interpretation have received careful textual and theological discussion.
The central truth is unmistakable across the New Testament: the crucified Redeemer is no mere creature.
The One who shed His human blood for our redemption is the divine Son.
This does not mean the divine nature itself bleeds.
It means the divine Son truly suffered and died in His assumed humanity.
The distinction is essential.
And so is the unity.
Without His genuine humanity, His suffering and death would not be truly human.
Without His genuine deity, we would not have the incarnate Son accomplishing the salvation Scripture attributes to Him.
The cross is not the story of God watching an unrelated innocent man die.
It is the story of the Father giving His beloved Son, and the Son willingly offering Himself in the power of the eternal Spirit (John 3:16; Hebrews 9:14).
And what a costly gift that was.
Because sin is not a minor mistake that God simply overlooks.
Sin is rebellion against the holy Creator.
It fractures our relationship with God.
It exposes our guilt.
It brings death.
And no amount of religious activity, moral improvement, charitable giving, or public respectability can erase our guilt before Him.
Romans 3:23 declares:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." (KJV)
All.
Not merely the scandalous.
Not merely the criminal.
Not merely the person whose sins became public.
The respected religious leader.
The successful professional.
The devoted parent.
The person who knows the right Scriptures but secretly cherishes the wrong desires.
And yes, the person writing these words.
Every one of us needs grace.
This is why the identity of Jesus matters so much.
We do not merely need better advice.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need forgiveness.
We need a Savior.
And Scripture tells us that the eternal Son became truly human to accomplish what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
The early church eventually expressed this biblical confession with extraordinary care.

At the Council of Chalcedon in AD 451, Christian leaders affirmed Jesus Christ as truly God and truly man, one and the same Son, acknowledged in two natures without confusion, change, division, or separation.
That confession did not create the deity or humanity of Jesus.
It sought to articulate faithfully what Scripture already taught and to guard against interpretations that denied either His full deity, His full humanity, or the unity of His Person.
The two natures are not blended into some third kind of being.
They are not separated into two competing persons.
Jesus is not fifty percent God and fifty percent man.
He is fully God and fully man, one Person, forever.
This is a claim about who Christ is, not a mathematical division of His identity.
And although the incarnation surpasses our complete comprehension, it does not require us to affirm that Jesus is God and not God in the same sense.
It calls us to distinguish carefully between His divine and human natures while confessing the unity of His Person.
There is humility in that.
Because finite minds should not expect to comprehend the infinite God exhaustively.
Yet neither should we call something irrational merely because it is beyond our full experience.
Scripture gives us enough to confess the truth faithfully, even where it does not explain every mystery of how the incarnation is possible.
But here is what I do not want you to miss.
The incarnation is not simply a doctrine to defend.
It is a revelation of the astonishing depth of God's redeeming love.
Think about the woman who believes her past has permanently disqualified her from grace.
Think about the father ashamed of the damage his anger has caused.
Think about the young person fighting temptation in secret.
Think about the believer who has fallen into the same sin so many times that repentance now feels embarrassing.
Think about the person who walked away from church because the people who spoke most loudly about holiness showed so little mercy.
Think about the skeptic who cannot reconcile the goodness of God with the suffering of the world.
The incarnation does not answer every question about suffering.
It does not promise that every wound will disappear in this lifetime.
It does not excuse sin or remove the need for repentance.
But it tells us something astonishing about the character of God.
The God who calls us to Himself is not indifferent to the brokenness of the world He came to redeem.
Jesus entered a world of grief.
He experienced rejection.
He was betrayed.
He endured injustice.
He suffered under human cruelty.
And He willingly bore the cross.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
"But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed." (KJV)
The Hebrew begins:
וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ
Vehu meḥolal mippeshaʿenu.
"But he was pierced/wounded because of our transgressions."
The Hebrew מְחֹלָל (meḥolal) conveys being wounded or pierced, while פְּשָׁעֵנוּ (peshaʿenu) refers to our transgressions or rebellious offenses.
In its broader context, Isaiah 53 describes the suffering servant bearing the iniquities of others.
Christians understand this prophecy in light of the suffering, death, and vindication of Jesus Christ, as the New Testament itself does in passages such as 1 Peter 2:24–25.
The healing Isaiah describes must not be reduced to a guarantee that every Christian will receive immediate physical healing.
The passage's central concern is the servant's redemptive suffering for sin and the peace and restoration that flow from it.
And that is precisely the kind of healing every sinner desperately needs.
Not merely a better public image.
Not merely temporary emotional relief.
Not merely the appearance of righteousness.
But forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
A restored relationship with God.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Because the Gospel does not pretend our sins are harmless.
It exposes them.
But it also announces that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Not to celebrate their rebellion.
Not to leave them imprisoned in shame.
But to call them to repentance, grant forgiveness, and transform their lives through His grace.
The same Jesus who told the truth about sin also welcomed repentant sinners.
The same Jesus who called people to deny themselves also invited the weary to come to Him.
The same Jesus who warned of judgment willingly gave Himself for the salvation of His people.
His grace is not permission to remain enslaved to sin.
His grace is the mercy that receives repentant sinners and begins to make them new.
And perhaps someone needs to hear this tonight.
You may have ruined your reputation.
You may have damaged relationships.
You may have betrayed someone's trust.
You may have spent years pretending that everything was fine while your private life was falling apart.
You may have convinced yourself that God is finished with you.
But the Gospel does not say that the worst thing you have done must become the final definition of who you are.
It says that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
It says that forgiveness is offered through Him.
It says that those who turn to Him in faith are not beyond the reach of His saving grace.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
Not because confession earns forgiveness.
Not because our tears pay for our sins.
Not because our promises can repair every consequence.
But because Jesus Christ is the righteous Savior whose sacrifice is sufficient.
And if the Son of God truly became human, truly died, and truly rose again, then redemption is not a sentimental religious slogan.
It is grounded in the historical and saving work of Jesus Christ.
There is another detail we cannot afford to overlook.
The incarnation did not end when Jesus rose from the dead.
The risen Christ was not merely a spirit.
He showed His disciples His hands and feet.
He invited them to recognize the reality of His resurrected body (Luke 24:39).
The eternal Son did not temporarily borrow humanity and then discard it when His mission was finished.
He rose bodily and ascended into heaven.
And Scripture continues to describe Him as the mediator between God and humanity.
First Timothy 2:5 says:
"For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." (KJV)
The glorified Savior remains truly human.
And truly divine.
The same Jesus who walked among sinners now reigns in glory.
The same Jesus who suffered is the risen Lord.
The same Jesus who interceded for His disciples continues as the great High Priest of His people.
This is why Hebrews 4:16 invites believers to approach the throne of grace with confidence, seeking mercy and help in time of need.
Not arrogance.
Not entitlement.
Confidence grounded in Christ.
Because the throne of grace belongs to the God who has provided a merciful and faithful High Priest.
And that changes how we pray.
When you confess your sins, you are not informing Jesus of something He did not know.
When you admit your weakness, you are not shocking Him.
When you come to Him exhausted, you are not approaching someone unfamiliar with human suffering.
But neither are you approaching someone powerless to help.
The Savior who knows what it means to suffer as a man possesses all the fullness of deity.
He is not less compassionate because He is God.
He is not less powerful because He became man.
And He is not less holy because He came near to sinners.
This is the glory of the incarnation.
The eternal Son truly became one of us without becoming sinful.
He entered our weakness without surrendering His divine power.
He endured death without ceasing to be the living God.
And He rose again, demonstrating His victory over death.
So can Jesus be fully human and fully divine without contradiction?
Yes.
Not because Christianity asks us to abandon reason.
Not because words have no meaning.
Not because contradictions become true when attached to religious language.
But because Scripture identifies one divine Person who possesses two distinct, complete natures.
The Son is truly God.
The Son became truly human.
His divine nature did not become a human nature.
His human nature did not become divine.
Neither nature was destroyed.
And His Person was not divided.
The incarnation is beyond our exhaustive comprehension, but the doctrine itself does not assert mutually exclusive properties of Christ in the same respect.
It is a mystery worthy of reverent study, not an excuse for careless thinking.
And once we begin to understand that, we discover why this truth has been cherished by Christians for centuries.
Because if Jesus were not truly human, He could not have lived and died as our human representative.
If Jesus were not truly divine, He would not be the eternal Son whose saving work reveals and accomplishes God's own redemption.
But Scripture presents Him as both.
The Word made flesh.
The fullness of deity dwelling bodily.
The merciful and faithful High Priest.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The only Savior.
And now the question moves from theology to your own heart.
What will you do with Jesus Christ?
You can admire the beauty of the incarnation and still refuse the One who became flesh.
You can defend orthodox doctrine and still cherish unrepented sin.
You can know the Greek words, quote the Hebrew Scriptures, explain the Council of Chalcedon, and impress an entire room with theological knowledge.
Yet none of that replaces personal repentance and faith in Christ.
Knowing facts about the Savior is not the same as trusting the Savior.
The Gospel calls us to more than intellectual agreement.
It calls us to turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ.
To abandon the illusion that we can save ourselves.
To receive His grace.
To follow Him.
And to let the truth of His death and resurrection reshape how we live.
Perhaps this article has challenged your understanding.
Perhaps it has confronted a secret sin.
Perhaps it has reminded you that the Savior you have been running from is the very Savior you desperately need.
If that is you, do not turn this moment into another passing emotional experience.
Pray.
Confess.
Repent.
Open the Scriptures.
Seek the fellowship of faithful believers.
And come to Christ.
You do not need to pretend that you understand every mystery before you can trust Him.
But you do need to recognize who He is and what He has done.
He is not a religious accessory to improve an otherwise self-directed life.
He is Lord.
He is Savior.
He is the eternal Son who became flesh.
And He is worthy of your trust, obedience, and worship.
If you are struggling to believe, bring your questions honestly to Scripture.
If you have been hiding sin, bring it into the light before God.
If you have wandered, turn back to Christ.
If you have been wounded, remember that your suffering is not invisible to Him.
And if you have been saved by grace, never let the wonder of the incarnation become ordinary.
Because the Son of God did not become human so that we could merely admire an impressive theological idea.
He came to seek and save the lost (Luke 19:10).
And the Gospel that announces His saving work is still worth proclaiming.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell forgiveness.
Not to turn the grace of God into merchandise.
But to help bring Scripture-centered teaching, encouragement, discipleship, and Gospel truth to people who need to hear about Jesus Christ.
There are people scrolling through Facebook right now who are silently questioning their faith.
Some are believers who have never understood why Jesus had to be both God and man.
Some are wounded Christians trying to find their way back.
Some are skeptics who have been told that the incarnation is logically impossible.
And some are carrying guilt so heavy that they no longer believe forgiveness could reach them.
Not because a Facebook share saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But because God can use the faithful communication of His Word to point people toward the Savior.
Because this truth deserves more than a passing glance.
It deserves to be studied, understood, defended faithfully, and treasured.
And I want to ask you something personally.
What moves you most deeply about the incarnation—that the eternal Son of God became truly human, that He understands our suffering, or that He willingly died to redeem sinners?
Not to impress anyone with a perfect theological answer.
But because your honest reflection may encourage someone else to open the Scriptures and seek Christ.
Your words may become the encouragement another person needs.
Not out of guilt.
And certainly not because financial support purchases His favor.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be voluntary, not reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And Philippians 4:15–17 shows Paul's appreciation for believers who partnered financially in Gospel ministry.
That is the spirit in which we invite you to partner with Gospel Warrior.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read, learn, share, pray, and grow.
Your value before God has never depended on your ability to give money.
For those who are able and willing to partner financially, however, your recurring support can help make continued content creation, biblical teaching, and wider Gospel outreach possible.
Those products can be meaningful reminders of faith, but they are never substitutes for prayer, Scripture, repentance, or fellowship with the church.
Our desire is not simply to gather an audience.
It is to help people grow in biblical understanding, spiritual maturity, and faithful discipleship.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person who is searching for answers.
Invite the skeptic willing to examine Christianity seriously.
Because the Gospel is too important to keep hidden behind our fear of what others might think.
And remember this.
Those things can help spread a message.
But the message itself is about someone infinitely greater than the ministry sharing it.
Jesus Christ.
The eternal Word.
The incarnate Son.
The sinless Savior.
The crucified Redeemer.
The risen Lord.
The merciful High Priest.
The One in whom all the fullness of deity dwells bodily.
The One who truly shared our humanity.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and faith.
The One who alone can reconcile us to God.
So the next time someone asks you how Jesus can be both fully God and fully man, do not be intimidated by the question.
Open John 1.
Read Colossians 2.
Study Hebrews 2.
Remember the distinction between Christ's two natures and the unity of His Person.
And then remember why it matters.
Because Christianity is not built upon the idea that humanity somehow climbed high enough to become divine.
It is built upon the astonishing announcement that the eternal Son of God came down to redeem humanity.
He entered our history.
He bore our suffering.
He carried our sins.
He died.
He rose.
And He remains the living Lord who saves.
The scandal of the cross was not the end of His story.
And through His grace, your sin does not have to be the end of yours.
The hands that once held the universe were pierced for sinners—and the risen Savior still holds out mercy to those who come to Him.
